title: PBW for an arbitrary-dimensional rational Lie algebra
statement:
Let $L$ be a rational Lie algebra [def-wf-lie-algebra], with no finite-dimensionality assumption. Let $U(L)$ and $j:L\to U(L)$ be the tensor-algebra quotient and its canonical linear map of [lem-sfb-enveloping-universal-property]: explicitly $T_{\mathbf Q}(L)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}L^{\otimes_{\mathbf Q}n}$ has concatenation multiplication, $U(L)$ is its quotient by the two-sided ideal generated by $x\otimes y-y\otimes x-[x,y]$ for $x,y\in L$, and $j$ is induced by degree one. For every rational vector-space basis $(e_b)_{b\in B}$ of $L$ and every total order on its index set $B$, the elements
$$j(e_{b_1})\cdots j(e_{b_n}),\qquad n\ge0,\quad b_1\le\cdots\le b_n,$$
indexed by the finite nondecreasing lists in $B$, form a rational vector-space basis of $U(L)$; the empty list contributes $1$. In particular, the canonical linear map $j:L\to U(L)$ is injective for every rational Lie algebra $L$. If $L=0$, the basis consists only of $1$ and $U(L)=\mathbf Q$.

source.place: Section 10j, construction on printed pp.199–200 and Theorem 10.36 (Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt), printed p.200; ordered-basis proof on pp.201–204. The theorem allows an arbitrary basis index set; the injectivity consequence is the independence of the degree-one monomials.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-tensor-word-basis] to the given basis $(e_b)_{b\in B}$, with no restriction on $B$, to identify $T_{\mathbf Q}(L)$ with the rational vector space on finite words in $B$, multiplied by concatenation. Write basis letters as $a,b,c$. For $u,v\in L$ put $r(u,v)=uv-vu-[u,v]$. Finite basis expansions and bilinearity give $r(u,v)=\sum_{a,b}u_a v_b r(a,b)$. Alternation [def-wf-lie-algebra] gives $r(a,a)=0$ and $r(a,b)=-r(b,a)$. Thus the defining ideal $J$ is generated by $r(a,b)$ for $a>b$. Its underlying vector space is the span of all $A r(a,b) C$, where $A,C$ are words: expand both multipliers in the word basis; conversely this span is closed under left and right multiplication by words and hence by all tensors.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, pp.200--201, tensor word basis and the displayed spanning relations for I(g).

proof.text: For a word $w$, let $|w|$ be its length and $\operatorname{inv}(w)$ the number of pairs of positions $i<j$ whose letters satisfy $w_i>w_j$. Define $v\prec w$ when $(|v|,\operatorname{inv}(v))$ is lexicographically smaller than $(|w|,\operatorname{inv}(w))$ in $\mathbf N^2$. This is a strict partial order, not necessarily total. It is well founded: in any nonempty set of words first minimize length and then inversion count. Use one rule for each adjacent inversion occurrence, $AabC\mapsto A(ba+[a,b])C$ with $a>b$. The swapped word has the same length and exactly one fewer inversion: cross comparisons with all other positions are unchanged in total. Each word in the finite expansion of the bracket term has length one less. Hence every right-side word is $\prec$ its leading word. The rule-relation span is $J$ by Step 1. Write $R_{\prec w}$ for the span of rule relations whose leading words are $\prec w$. We check the ambiguity hypothesis below. This rank uses only finite words, so the given total order on $B$ need not be well founded.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, printed pp.201--202, length and inversion reductions; repaired by using the lexicographic pair on single words, not the printed measure on sums.

proof.text: Two rules at the same position agree. For disjoint positions write $w=AabCuvD$ with $a>b$ and $u>v$, and put $p=ba+[a,b]$, $q=vu+[u,v]$. The first reducts are $ApCuvD$ and $AabCqD$. Compare each with $ApCqD$: their differences are $ApC r(u,v)D$ and $A r(a,b)CqD$. Expand $p,q$ into words. The leading word of every resulting contextual relation is smaller than $w$: either one other adjacent inversion has been swapped, lowering the inversion count by one without changing length, or a bracket has shortened the word. Both differences lie in $R_{\prec w}$. This includes adjacent disjoint pairs ($C$ empty).

source.place: Theorem 10.36, p.202, Step 4 disjoint reductions; explicit lower-relation calculation by Q12.

proof.text: The remaining distinct positions overlap in three consecutive letters $a>b>c$. Suppress the common prefix and suffix. Reducing the left pair first gives $bac+[a,b]c$; swapping $ac$ and then $bc$ in its cubic term gives $$P=cba+[b,c]a+b[a,c]+[a,b]c.$$ Reducing the right pair first gives $acb+a[b,c]$; swapping $ac$ and then $ab$ gives $$Q=cba+c[a,b]+[a,c]b+a[b,c].$$ The relations used after the first reductions lead at $bac,bca,acb,cab$. Each of these is a permutation of $abc$ with fewer inversions. Restoring the common context does not change this inequality: all cross inversions depend only on the multiset of the three letters, which is unchanged. Therefore the difference of the first reducts is congruent to $P-Q$ modulo $R_{\prec w}$ for the original contextual word $w$.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, pp.202--203, Step 4 overlapping reductions; track the leading words explicitly.

proof.text: In the tensor algebra, direct expansion gives $$P-Q=r([b,c],a)+r(b,[a,c])+r([a,b],c)+[[b,c],a]+[b,[a,c]]+[[a,b],c].$$ The last three terms vanish by skew-symmetry and Jacobi [def-wf-lie-algebra]: their sum is $-[a,[b,c]]-[b,[c,a]]-[c,[a,b]]$. Each of the first three terms expands by Step 1 into finitely many multiples of $r(e_i,e_j)$ with $i>j$. After restoring the prefix and suffix, their leading words have length one less than $w$, regardless of which basis indices occur in the bracket expansions. They lie in $R_{\prec w}$. Together with Steps 3 and 4 this proves compatibility for all rules with the same leading word. There are no other cases: two distinct adjacent pairs are either disjoint or overlap once, and two overlapping inversions force $a>b>c$.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, p.203, Jacobi calculation in Step 4; replace mere congruence modulo the entire ideal by congruence modulo smaller relations.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-triangular-linear-relations] with $k=\mathbf Q$, $W$ the finite words in $B$, the strict partial order of Step 2 and all contextual adjacent-inversion rules. Right-side supports are finite and strictly lower by Step 2; compatibility modulo smaller relations is Steps 3--5. Its subspace $R$ is exactly $J$ by Step 1, so the quotient is the stated $U(L)$. The words with no rule occurrence are exactly the nondecreasing lists: adjacent inequalities imply every earlier letter is at most every later letter by transitivity of the given total order. Conversely such a list has no adjacent inversion. The cited criterion gives their classes as a rational basis of $U(L)$, including the empty word as $1$.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, pp.203--204, Steps 5--8; agent repair using the explicit triangular linear-relations criterion.

proof.text: For the given basis, if $x=\sum_b q_b e_b$ has $j(x)=0$, then $\sum_b q_b j(e_b)=0$. The one-letter words are distinct members of the basis proved in Step 6, so all the finitely many coefficients $q_b$ vanish and $x=0$. Thus $j$ is injective. This applies to every rational Lie algebra: [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-free] supplies a basis, and classical choice permits a total order on its index set. When $L=0$, its basis index set is empty, the only word is empty, and no relation occurs. The tensor word algebra and its quotient are $\mathbf Q$, with sole basis element $1$.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, printed p.200, degree-one consequence and empty-basis case of the construction; vector-space basis existence is Stacks 09FN.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 10.36, printed pp.200--204, with the reduction argument repaired using the existing triangular linear-relations criterion and length/inversion rank on words.
